# IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 — introductions lesson

**Source:** IELTS Advantage, [IELTS Writing Task 1 Introductions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1IVFRWCpNxE), 13 m 20 s.  
**Transcript:** auto-generated English captions exported and reviewed (156 lines; captions reach 13:16 of a 13:20 video). The lesson proposes a quick paraphrase method for Task 1 introductions and names several patterns the instructor says he found in Cambridge books.

## The useful core

An introduction should identify what the visual presents, while an overview states its main features and detail paragraphs support them. Understand the task and visual first; then write a concise, accurate description of the subject, measure, place or group, and time period that matter. One sentence is usually enough. It is fine to repeat a precise term from the task when a supposed synonym would be less accurate.

The instructor builds an introduction from three common elements: the kind of visual, the subject being measured, and the time reference. He demonstrates changing sentence structure and word form as well as using synonyms. The transferable principle is to paraphrase only where the new wording preserves the task’s meaning and sounds natural. A word should not be changed merely to make the introduction look more sophisticated.

### Reusable routine

1. Read the complete task and identify the visual type, subject, unit or measure, groups or place, and time period.
2. Say in plain language what the visual shows before editing any wording.
3. Write a concise opening that preserves those facts. Keep a key noun or exact year if that is the clearest choice.
4. Check that the subject and verb agree, the wording does not add an unsupported category, and the report still needs a separate overview and selected details.
5. Practise on varied charts, tables, maps, and processes; compare revisions against the visual and receive criteria-based feedback.

## Instructor examples and limits

- **Visual labels:** the instructor often replaces chart/table/graph with “data” and uses “illustration” for maps, diagrams, or processes. These are optional substitutions, not a template. Name the visual accurately where that is clearer; “illustration” can be vague, and sentences using “data” need correct agreement and a natural construction.
- **Reporting verbs:** “shows,” “presents,” “demonstrates,” and “displays” can work in suitable contexts. Do not swap them mechanically; preserve the relationship between the visual, the subject, and the information.
- **People and groups:** select a description that matches the context (for example, residents, visitors, or workers). Do not force nationality labels, slang, or a synonym whose meaning you are unsure of; a clear phrase such as “people from [place]” is safer than an inaccurate demonym.
- **Time:** exact years and ranges often need no paraphrase. The lesson swaps “between X and Y” with “from X to Y”; use a swap only if the dates and endpoints remain identical.
- **One sentence:** a short introduction is often sufficient, but sentence count is not an IELTS rule. Avoid filler and do not insert information absent from the task.
- **Practice:** the lesson recommends varied practice and feedback. Feedback can come from a qualified teacher, a reliable rubric, or careful self-review; the video’s suggestion that “perfect practice” requires an expert is coaching advice, not an official condition.

## Claims to keep out of course policy

The instructor reports percentages for visual types and time references based on his review of Cambridge books (for example, chart/table/graph/map/diagram/plan frequencies and the prevalence of time periods). The video does not identify the editions or question count, nor show its coding rules or calculations. Treat these figures as an unverified description of his dataset, not a forecast of what a candidate will receive. The categories may also overlap in ordinary language.

The “Band 9” title is promotional framing; the demonstration does not independently establish a score or guarantee an outcome. The reliable lesson is accuracy and relevance: paraphrase meaningfully, do not overcomplicate the sentence, and do not memorize a pattern that breaks when the task includes an unexpected group or qualifier.

### Overlapping companion Short — `JUYxr4lTpJQ`

The 42-second [Easy Way to Paraphrase IELTS Task 1 Writing Short](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JUYxr4lTpJQ) repeats the Cambridge-book pattern claim and gives a brief worked formula: change “chart” to “data,” “shows” to “displays,” “percentage” to “proportion,” describe people with a country demonym, and change “between” dates to “from … to …”. Its auto-generated captions stop at 0:37 of 0:42, mid-sentence. It adds no separate method to the longer lesson. Treat every substitution as conditional: preserve the actual population, use a demonym only if it is accurate, maintain natural subject–verb agreement, and check that the dates and endpoints are unchanged. The frequency claim remains unverified.

### Related Short — understand the visual before writing

The 23-second [Start Your IELTS Task 1 Essay Right: The Key Step You’re Missing! Short](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/NM0WmA51SEY) advises learners to inspect and understand a line graph before drafting, because a report cannot be accurate if its writer has not understood the visual. Auto-captions cover the core point through 0:20 of 0:23. This reinforces the longer beginner course’s prompt-and-visual reading routine; it is a reminder, not a distinct scoring rule.

## Course integration

Teach the introduction as one part of the whole report: identify the task accurately, state the main pattern in an overview, then select and compare enough details. An opening is not a substitute for overview and detail writing. The official task asks candidates to summarize and report the main features and requires at least 150 words; IELTS does not prescribe this video's introduction formula or a fixed introduction length. ([IELTS Academic Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-writing); [IELTS Writing key assessment criteria](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf))
